common_name: Archie Owen Spuria Iris (Nies Medal Bright Yellow Spuria Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall so roots establish before winter; Archie Owen, bred by Ben Hager and registered in 1970, went on to win the American Iris Society's Nies Medal in 1973.

directions: Set rhizomes shallowly, just below the soil surface, in rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Archie Owen carries stiffly upright, self-colored bright yellow flowers on tall stems above sword-like foliage in midseason, and its clean, unmarked color has kept it a benchmark yellow spuria for decades. Water generously from fall through the spring bloom period, then withhold water during the plant's summer dormancy in July and August to prevent rot. Unlike bearded iris, spurias are heavy feeders and resent disturbance, so fertilize in early spring and only divide crowded clumps every four to six years, expecting a year or two before rebloom resumes at full strength.

common_name: Imperial Bronze Spuria Iris (Deep Bronze Brown-Veined Spuria Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall in full sun; Imperial Bronze was bred by Eleanor McCown from 'Driftwood' x 'Imperial Night' and registered in 1970.

directions: Plant rhizomes just beneath the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Imperial Bronze produces vivid yellow flowers so heavily veined and overlaid with brown that the overall effect reads as a rich, smoky bronze, accented by a small yellow signal patch, on tall midseason stems above narrow, ribbed foliage. Keep the planting consistently moist from autumn through the spring bloom season, then let the soil dry out through the plant's midsummer dormancy, since standing water at that time invites rhizome rot. Established clumps are long-lived and need little attention beyond an early-spring feeding, and should be left undisturbed for several years before dividing crowded groups after bloom.

common_name: Sultan's Sash Spuria Iris (Nies Medal Red-Violet and Gold Spuria Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall in full sun; Sultan's Sash was bred by O. David Niswonger from 'Cinnamon Stick' x 'Redwood Supreme', introduced in 1990, and later won the Nies Medal in 1999.

directions: Set rhizomes shallowly in rich, neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun, as with tall bearded iris. Sultan's Sash bears deep red-violet flowers infused with gold on the falls, a striking, jewel-toned break from the yellow and blue tones common among spurias, and its award record made it a widely grown standard-bearer for the color class. Provide steady moisture from fall regrowth through the midseason bloom, then cut back watering during the summer dormant period to keep rhizomes from rotting. Feed generously in early spring since spurias require more fertility than bearded iris, and leave clumps undisturbed for several years, since they resent frequent digging and rebloom slowly after division.

common_name: Protégé Spuria Iris (Compact Nonfading True Blue Spuria Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall in full sun; Protégé was bred by Ben Hager using Iris spuria subsp. carthaliniae parentage to bring a truer, nonfading blue into spuria breeding lines.

directions: Plant rhizomes just below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Protégé is noticeably more compact than most garden spurias, reaching about three feet, and carries a clear, nonfading true blue that holds its tone in strong sun far better than many older spuria hybrids. Keep soil evenly moist from fall through the midseason bloom period, then allow it to dry through the summer dormancy that follows flowering to avoid rot. Because its carthaliniae heritage gives it a naturally tidy habit, it works well toward the front of a spuria planting; fertilize in early spring and divide only when clumps become congested, since transplant shock can delay bloom for a season or two.
